Compost is a dark, crumbly, rich material made from rotted organic matter — things like food scraps, leaves, and plant waste — that has broken down naturally over time. Think of it as nature's own recycled fertilizer. It looks and smells something like very healthy, dark soil, but it is not soil itself. It is something you add to soil to make it far more nourishing for plants.

Compost comes from organic materials, meaning things that were once alive. Common ingredients include:

  • Kitchen waste — fruit and vegetable peels, coffee grounds, tea bags, eggshells, leftover plant-based food
  • Garden waste — dried leaves, grass clippings, plant stems, flowers
  • Paper-based materials — torn-up cardboard, newspaper (in small amounts)

What you cannot use to make compost: meat, dairy, cooked oily food, or anything synthetic. Those either don't break down properly or attract pests and create harmful conditions.

When you pile up organic waste and leave it under the right conditions — some moisture, some air, and warmth — tiny living things get to work. Bacteria, fungi, and other microorganisms begin eating and digesting the material. Earthworms and insects also help. Over weeks or months, all that organic matter slowly decomposes, breaking down into a uniform, stable substance. That substance is compost.

This transformation process is called composting. Compost is the finished product of that process — the point where the original materials are no longer recognizable and have turned into something entirely new and useful.
What It Looks and Smells Like

Finished compost is:

  • Dark brown or almost black in color
  • Loose and crumbly in texture (not wet, not dry — slightly moist, like a wrung-out sponge)
  • Earthy in smell — it smells like a forest floor after rain, not like rotting food

If compost smells foul or looks slimy, it means the process didn't go right. Good compost has a clean, pleasant, earthy scent.

Compost is primarily used in gardening and farming. Here's what it does:

1. Feeds the soil with nutrients.
As compost is made of broken-down organic matter, it is packed with nutrients — nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, and many trace minerals — that plants need to grow. When you mix compost into soil, you are essentially feeding the soil, which in turn feeds your plants.

2. Improves soil structure.
Sandy soil doesn't hold water well; heavy clay soil becomes hard and compact. Compost improves both. It makes sandy soil hold moisture better, and it loosens heavy clay soil so roots can breathe and spread more easily.

3. Supports soil life.
Healthy soil is full of microorganisms — millions of bacteria and fungi per handful — that help plants absorb nutrients. Compost feeds and encourages this community of life, making the soil a living, active ecosystem rather than just an inert medium.

4. Acts as a mulch.
Compost can be spread on top of the soil around plants (a practice called mulching). This layer protects the soil from drying out, regulates temperature, and slowly releases nutrients as rain or watering washes through it.

5. Reduces the need for chemical fertilizers.
Because compost naturally supplies nutrients, gardens and farms that use compost regularly often need far less (or no) artificial fertilizer.

Compost comes in two main forms:

  • Homemade compost — made in a compost bin or pile in someone's backyard or kitchen. This is common among gardeners and environmentally conscious households.
  • Bagged or commercial compost — sold in garden centers and hardware stores, already processed and ready to use. Labels often say things like "garden compost," "organic compost," or "multi-purpose compost."

Some municipalities collect food and garden waste from households and process it on a large scale, then sell or distribute the resulting compost back to residents or farms. This is called municipal composting.

Compost has a larger environmental significance as well.

When organic waste — food scraps, yard clippings — ends up in a landfill, it breaks down in an airless environment and produces methane, a potent greenhouse gas. Composting diverts this waste from landfills and turns it into something beneficial instead. This is why composting is widely considered an important environmental practice, not just a gardening one.

In short, compost closes a loop: things that grew from the earth, fed by nutrients in the soil, are broken back down and returned to the earth as nutrients once more.
Compost is a dark, crumbly, nutrient-rich material formed from the natural decomposition of organic waste (like food scraps and plant matter), used to enrich soil and support healthy plant growth.
